newsitem.title: CHILE: Latin American socialists rap free-market policies.
newsitem.headline: Latin American socialists rap free-market policies.

text.p: Latin American socialists, including some of the region's top left-wing politicians, have launched a sharp critique on free-market economic policies blamed for worsening poverty and social tensions.

The Socialist International's Committee for Latin America and the Caribbean, meeting in the Chilean capital over the weekend, said women have been especially hard hit by the consequences of neo-liberal economic thinking in vogue from Argentina to Mexico.

"Neo-liberal policies generate, more often than not, grave social conflicts as a consequence of sharp concentration of wealth and an increase in poverty," said the socialist leaders in a statement issued late on Saturday.

They blamed neo-liberal policies, which usually include privatisation of state companies and leaner government spending, for worsening "the lack of opportunities for important sectors of the population."
"The women of Latin America and the Caribbean have been especially affected by this phenomenon, becoming 'the poorest of the poor,'" said the statement, entitled the Declaration of Santiago.

Nearly every country in Latin America, with the notable exception of Cuba, has whittled down the size of its state or instituted other free-market reforms in recent years to reduce deficits and inflation and attract foreign investment.
Most of the delegates at the Santiago meeting had the word "former" attached to their titles, perhaps reflecting the region's current trend away from big-government policies.

Delegates included former Argentine president Raul Alfonsin, former Nicaraguan interior minister Tomas Borge, and former presidential candidates Leonel Brizola and Francisco Pena Gomez of Brazil and the Dominican Republic, respectively.

Delegates also urged the United States to end its policy of certifying whether countries are cooperating in the fight against drug trafficking, saying it was driving the two sides apart when they should be cooperating.

"We call on the United States to work together with producer countries and end certification, because it's a one-sided practice that does not contribute to a solution to this problem," said Pena Gomez, president of the committee.
"Drug trafficking must be contained, and that requires more action by governments and better police work, but also better coordination between producer and consumer countries," he said.
